Your call, once reconciled.

📚 Today you learned

Nasdaq Listing Standards & Delisting (The Minimum Equity Rule)

Every Nasdaq-listed company has to keep clearing minimum bars — usually $2.5-5M in stockholders' equity (or alternative tests: market value of listed shares, or net income) plus a $1 minimum bid price. Miss it, and Nasdaq issues a deficiency letter with a cure period (typically 180 days, sometimes extended). DRCT just ran out of that clock: it failed to restore its equity threshold by Oct 1, got a delisting determination, and is being bumped to OTC Pink "Limited Information" — a thinner, less liquid market where spreads widen and many brokers restrict buying. This is unique to exchange-listed equities; forex pairs and major indices don't have an equivalent "you've been kicked off the venue" mechanism. The lesson for your book: a stock trading at single digits with negative equity and heavy cash burn isn't just fundamentally weak — it can lose its listing entirely, and once that happens the position becomes hard to exit cleanly even if you wanted to. None of your current holdings are anywhere near this risk (GOOG, SPXC are both large/mid-cap with healthy balance sheets), but it's exactly the kind of tail risk to screen out before adding any sub-$5 momentum name from stock-finder.

Also today: Reverse stock split — a company shrinks its share count (e.g., 1-for-10) to artificially boost its per-share price back above the $1 Nasdaq minimum without changing market cap; often a last resort before delisting, and frequently a bearish signal despite the "higher" price.
